title: How can we draw a bigger and a smaller copy of a rectangle?
description: One rectangle is redrawn smaller and then bigger by multiplying both sides by a single factor. A classmate picks another factor, and every drawing is checked by dividing each new side by the old side.
teaching_notes: One idea: any single factor on both sides gives a rectangle of the same shape, so different drawings can all be right. Watch for students who think only one size is correct.

source: Figure it Out (ratios and proportions, question 5)
video_script.why: The child sees that many different drawings keep the same shape, and that the one thing they share is a single factor on both sides.
video_script.substitution: Pick one number, multiply the width and the height by it, and divide new by old to check.
video_script.anchor: a rectangle redrawn smaller and bigger in a notebook
video_script.payoff_line: Drawings of different sizes are all correct, as long as both sides change by the same factor.

final_answer.value: Yes, all the drawings are correct
final_answer.spoken: yes, drawings of different sizes are all correct when both sides change by the same factor

maths_rules: sample rectangle used to show the method (the book's figure has no stated scale): 6 cm wide, 4 cm high
smaller: factor 1/2; 6 × 1/2 = 3 and 4 × 1/2 = 2; so 3 cm by 2 cm
bigger: factor 2; 6 × 2 = 12 and 4 × 2 = 8; so 12 cm by 8 cm
a classmate: factor 3/2; 6 × 3/2 = 9 and 4 × 3/2 = 6; so 9 cm by 6 cm
video_script.design: One idea: one factor on both sides keeps the shape, so many sizes are right. Uses the factor of change from the solved example. The notebook rectangle stays for the whole video.
open_questions: The book's rectangle has no stated size, so the video shows the method on a sample rectangle of 6 cm by 4 cm. The child then measures the book's own rectangle.

<bookmark mark='less'/>A factor less than one makes the rectangle smaller.
<bookmark mark='more'/>A factor more than one makes it bigger.

narration: <bookmark mark='f'/>Step one, for a smaller rectangle choose the factor one half.
<bookmark mark='w'/>Six times one half is three.
<bookmark mark='h'/>Four times one half is two.
<bookmark mark='draw'/>We draw a rectangle three centimetres by two centimetres.

narration: <bookmark mark='f'/>Step two, for a bigger rectangle choose the factor two.
<bookmark mark='w'/>Six times two is twelve.
<bookmark mark='h'/>Four times two is eight.
<bookmark mark='draw'/>We draw a rectangle twelve centimetres by eight centimetres.

narration: <bookmark mark='f'/>Step three, a classmate may choose the factor three halves.
<bookmark mark='w'/>Six times three halves is nine.
<bookmark mark='h'/>Four times three halves is six.
<bookmark mark='draw'/>That drawing is nine centimetres by six centimetres, and it is different from ours.

marks.chk: the words Check: new ÷ old are written

narration: <bookmark mark='chk'/>Step four, divide each new side by the old side to check.
<bookmark mark='one'/>Three divided by six and two divided by four are both one half.
<bookmark mark='two'/>Twelve divided by six and eight divided by four are both two.
<bookmark mark='three'/>Nine divided by six and six divided by four are both three halves.

beats.on_screen: Answer: all are correct, each with one factor on both sides
